regions.labelEs: PERO CUÁNTO SE TARDA EN LEER UN TAC

applications.explanationEn: Cuánto asks about the amount of time.
Se leaves the person unspecified, and tarda uses the matching singular form.
Tarda gives the time required, en introduces the activity, and leer stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: ASÍ QUE EL AÑO QUE VIENE TENÉIS QUE VENIROS DE VISITA A LA MONTAÑA Y TAM

applications.explanationEn: The two words work together as a connector introducing the resulting plan.
This fixed time expression uses viene after año to identify next year.
Tenéis carries the person and time, que links it to the action, and veniros remains the dictionary form with os attached.
The -éis ending addresses more than one familiar person.
The attached os refers back to the familiar plural listeners.
Veniros keeps venir in its dictionary form and attaches os to mark the familiar plural group.
Veniros supplies motion toward the speaker, while de visita marks the purpose as a visit.
The complete expression identifies the coming year.

regions.labelEs: ME DUELE EL DEDO GORDO Y HE LEÍDO SOBRE UN CASO EN EL QUE EL DOLOR DE DEDO GORDO ERA UNA SEÑAL DE METÁSTASIS

applications.explanationEn: Me identifies the speaker as the person feeling the pain, while singular duele agrees with the one thing that hurts.
The adjective follows dedo and the two words conventionally identify the big toe.
He carries the first-person present form of haber, and leído is the unchanged past-participle form of leer.
En comes before the article el and que to relate the case to what happened in it.
The same conventional two-word expression names the big toe.
Era uses the imperfect form for a past state that serves as background to the case.

regions.labelEs: PERO NO TE DISTE UN GOLPE AYER EN EL DEDO

applications.exampleEs: PERO NO TE DISTE UN GOLPE AYER EN EL DEDO
applications.explanationEn: The ordinary negative statement order remains in place; the surrounding question marks and intonation turn the complete clause into a yes-or-no question.
Te marks that the bump happened to the listener, diste changes dar for that past event, and un golpe names the bump.
Diste presents the bump as one completed past event.

regions.labelEs: SÍ PERO Y SI NO TIENE RELACIÓN

applications.explanationEn: The two words open an anxious “what if” possibility.
Si introduces a possibility, and tiene stays in the ordinary present form because it is treated as genuinely possible.

regions.labelEs: CUANDO ESTIMARON TUS PROBABILIDADES DE SUPERVIVENCIA CREO QUE HICIERON SUPOSICIONES OPTIMISTAS SOBRE TUS AFICIONES

applications.explanationEn: Optimistas follows suposiciones in the neutral noun-then-description order.
Both words are plural, so optimistas uses its plural -s ending.
Estimaron presents the estimate as one completed past event.
Hicieron presents making the assumptions as a completed past event.

regions.labelEs: SEGURAMENTE NO SEA NADA PERO DADOS TUS ANTECEDENTES VAMOS A PEDIR UN TAC COMPLETO YA TE LLAMAREMOS CON LOS RESULTADOS INTENTA NO PREOCUPARTE MIENTRAS

applications.explanationEn: The ending -mente turns segura into an adverb describing how certain the speaker is.
No appears before sea because nada follows the verb; the two negatives reinforce one negative meaning.
Dados agrees in masculine plural with antecedentes and introduces that medical history as the reason for the decision.
Vamos carries the first-person plural present form, a links it to the action, and pedir stays in its dictionary form.
TAC is the medical scan noun, and completo follows it in the neutral noun-then-description order.
Completo uses masculine singular -o to match the understood masculine singular scan name TAC.
Te replaces the person who will receive the call and appears directly before the changed future verb llamaremos.
Intenta directly tells one familiar person what to do.
Intenta changes into a familiar command, while preocuparte remains the unchanged action form despite the intervening no.
Preocuparte keeps the dictionary form preocupar and attaches te for the familiar listener.
Llamaremos keeps the full dictionary form llamar and adds the first-person plural future ending -emos.

applications.explanationEn: Cuesta presents the action as difficult, and creer stays in its unchanged dictionary form as that action.
Hace comes before the completed duration seis años to place the situation that far in the past.
Estaba uses the imperfect form for the earlier background state.
Estaba presents the speaker's earlier condition, and calva names that condition.
Calva uses feminine singular -a because the speaker describes herself as a woman.
Largo comes before camino to present the journey as an evaluated long experience.
Largo uses masculine singular -o to match camino.

applications.exampleEs: ME PAREZCO A LA NIÑA DE THE RING
applications.explanationEn: Me matches the speaker, parezco changes for that speaker, and a introduces the full comparison target la niña de The Ring.
The repeated s letters stretch the threatening hiss on the page.
The question marks and hesitant intonation turn the describing word bueno into a yes-or-no confirmation question.

regions.labelEs: CREES QUE YA ESTÁN LO BASTANTE SOCIALIZADOS

applications.exampleEs: CREES QUE YA ESTÁN LO BASTANTE SOCIALIZADOS
applications.explanationEn: The statement-shaped clause keeps its ordinary order; the surrounding question marks and intonation turn it into a yes-or-no question.
Lo bastante sets the required degree, and socializados names the resulting quality.

regions.labelEs: ESTE PUEDE QUE NECESITE OTRA CARICIA

applications.explanationEn: Puede que introduces uncertainty, so necesitar changes to necesite instead of necesita.

excludedUnits.rationale: RABBIT RESCUE is a readable English organization sign, not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: The words keep ordinary statement order; the surrounding question marks and intonation turn them into a yes-or-no question without an extra helper word.
Ha carries the present form for an unspecified singular person, and visto is the unchanged past-participle form of ver.
The repeated e letters prolong the excited shout as the wheelbarrow rolls.
The short proposal becomes a yes-or-no question through its question marks and intonation, without needing a separate helper word.

regions.labelEs: NO TENEMOS QUE MADRUGAR LOS DOS

applications.exampleEs: NO TENEMOS QUE MADRUGAR LOS DOS
applications.explanationEn: The ordinary negative statement order remains in place; the surrounding question marks and intonation turn the complete clause into a yes-or-no question.
Tenemos carries the first-person plural present form, que links it to the action, and madrugar stays in its dictionary form.
The repeated n and g letters stretch the reluctant groan.
Buena commonly comes before idea when judging it positively.
Buena uses feminine singular -a to match idea.

regions.labelEs: JA LES GUSTAN MÁS MIS SEMILLAS

applications.explanationEn: Les marks the rabbits as the group experiencing the preference, and gustan is plural because mis semillas names more than one liked thing.

regions.labelEs: OYE CÓMO LE HAGO UNA FOTO A ESTE

applications.explanationEn: Oye directly gets the attention of one familiar listener.
Cómo asks for the method.

applications.exampleEs: LE HAGO UNA FOTO A ESTE
applications.explanationEn: Hago una foto names taking a picture, le anticipates the subject being photographed, and a este makes that subject explicit.

regions.labelEs: TE TRAIGO TÉ DE LIMÓN Y MIEL MÁS ALMOHADAS UNA NAPOLITANA IBUPROFENO OTRA MANTA UN
SOLO ERA UNA APENDICITIS EN SERIO ESTOY

applications.explanationEn: The two words form the fixed expression used to insist that the speaker is serious.
Era uses the imperfect form to describe the earlier medical state.

regions.labelEs: ME TOCA CUIDAR DE TI Y LO VOY A HACER BIEN

applications.explanationEn: Me marks the person whose turn or responsibility it is, toca stays singular, and cuidar names the action.
Cuidar de is the reusable pattern for looking after someone, and ti names the listener after the preposition.
Lo replaces the already mentioned act of caring and appears directly before the changed finite verb voy.
Voy carries the first-person singular present form, a links it to the action, and hacer stays in its dictionary form.
The two words form a common exclamation of surprise or exasperation.
The second speaker uses the same common exclamation of surprise or exasperation.
Para directly tells one familiar person to stop.

regions.labelEs: QUINCE AÑOS SIN RASTRO DEL CÁNCER

applications.explanationEn: Sin rastro de forms the conventional no-trace expression, and de plus el contracts to del before cáncer.

regions.labelEs: SÍ QUE TENGO ALGUNOS SÍNTOMAS RAROS DOLOR EN LAS ARTICULACIONES FATIGA CREO QUE ESTOY PERDIENDO LA VISTA DE CERCA

applications.explanationEn: Sí que strongly confirms the following verb tengo.
Raros follows síntomas in the neutral noun-then-description order.
Raros uses masculine plural -os to match síntomas.
Estoy carries the first-person present form, and perdiendo names the action in progress.
Perdiendo supplies the changing form of perder, and la vista completes the conventional expression for losing eyesight.
The two words form the fixed expression for seeing something at close range.
Nos matches the speakers, hacemos changes hacerse for “we,” and viejos names the resulting condition.
The three words form a modest positive assessment: something is not as bad as it might have been.
Lo que introduces an unspecified thing described by the following verb.
Todo supplies the complete extent, lo que forms the conventional relative expression, and quería fills the verb slot by stating what the speaker wanted.

cards.questionEn: How do you exclaim “my God”?
cards.noteEn: Dios mío can express shock, frustration, or a literal address to God. Mío follows Dios and agrees with its masculine form.
Biiip imitates a sustained electronic tone. Spanish sound spellings vary, and extra i letters make the tone feel longer.

cards.promptEs: letras repetidas para alargar una voz
cards.questionEn: How can informal writing show that a speaker holds a sound for a long time?
cards.answerEn: Repeat the letter that represents the stretched sound.
cards.noteEn: This is expressive spelling used in comics, messages, and informal writing, not a standard dictionary form. More repeated letters usually suggest a longer or stronger shout: vamos can become vamooos.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?

cards.answerEn: people; one; you in general (impersonal marker)
cards.noteEn: Before a third-person singular verb, se can leave the people doing the action unspecified.

cards.promptEs: se + verbo en tercera persona singular (persona no especificada)
cards.questionEn: How can Spanish describe what people in general, an unspecified person, or ‘you’ generally do?
cards.answerEn: Put se before a third-person singular verb and leave the person unspecified.
cards.noteEn: This impersonal pattern focuses on the action rather than naming who performs it: aquí se trabaja means ‘people work here.’ It is distinct from the reflexive use in which someone acts on themself.

example.es: En esta biblioteca se estudia en silencio.
example.en: People study quietly in this library.

cards.noteEn: Tarda is a present form of tardar for one person or thing. Tardar en followed by an action says that the action takes time.

example.en: The train takes a while to arrive.

cards.promptEs: tardar + tiempo + en + acción en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say how long someone takes to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tardar, optionally give the amount of time, then en and the action in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The action form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and can carry an attached pronoun: tardaron una hora en llegar; tardan mucho en darse cuenta. Use cuánto to ask the amount of time.

example.en: They took two hours to arrive.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links tardar to the action that takes time
cards.noteEn: Tardar uses en before an action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: She took an hour to reply.

cards.noteEn: TAC abbreviates tomografía axial computarizada, a CT scan. The full name is feminine, so una TAC is often preferred; un TAC is especially common in Spain and among medical professionals.

example.en: I need a CT scan of my abdomen.

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.

cards.answerEn: cancer, pronounced with an exaggerated long vowel
cards.noteEn: The standard word is cáncer. Extra a letters show that the stressed vowel is being drawn out for comic emphasis; the written accent stays on the first á.

cards.promptEs: dos años · siete años · diez años · quince años
cards.questionEn: Why does the strip revisit scenes separated by two, seven, ten, and fifteen years?
cards.answerEn: It presents a long cancer-survival retrospective, moving from treatment and uncertainty toward fifteen years without a recurrence.
cards.noteEn: The grayscale panels reprise earlier stages of diagnosis, treatment, recurrence anxiety, and milestones. The newer scenes add ordinary shared life, aging, and care. The final fifteen-year marker makes survival itself—not a conventional punch line—the emotional culmination.

cards.answerEn: so; therefore (as part of así que)

cards.questionEn: How do you connect a situation to its result with “so”?
cards.answerEn: Use así que before the result.
cards.noteEn: Así que joins a cause or situation to what follows from it. The two words work together as one connector; translating así and que separately will not give the intended meaning.

example.es: Está lloviendo, así que llevo un paraguas.
example.en: It is raining, so I am carrying an umbrella.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a result connector

cards.questionEn: How do you say “next year” by describing the year that is coming?
cards.noteEn: The relative word que links año to viene, “comes.” The same pattern works with other time nouns: la semana que viene and el mes que viene. Viene stays singular because it describes one week, month, or year.
Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Viene is the present form of venir for one subject. In a phrase such as el mes que viene, the coming month is the next one.

example.es: Nos mudamos el mes que viene.

cards.answerEn: you all have (informal plural, mainly Spain)
cards.noteEn: Tenéis is the present form of tener for vosotros or vosotras. It informally addresses more than one person and is used especially in Spain.

example.en: Do you all have the tickets?

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”
to come; to come over (addressing several people)
cards.noteEn: Veniros is venir plus os, the marker for informal plural vosotros in Spain. After tenéis que, it stays in this unchanged action form.

example.en: You all have to come over this summer.

cards.questionEn: Where does me, te, se, nos, or os go when a verb used with one of those words stays in its dictionary form?
cards.answerEn: Attach the matching small word to the end: unir + me becomes unirme.
cards.noteEn: A pronominal verb is learned with se, such as unirse or acostarse. When its action verb remains in the unchanged dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, replace se with the form that matches the person and write it as part of the same word: acostarme, unirte, or irnos.

example.en: I want to go to bed early.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone goes or comes for a visit?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir or venir followed by de visita.
cards.noteEn: Only ir or venir changes for the person and time. The fixed words de visita identify the purpose as visiting, and natural English usually supplies “for a visit.”

example.en: Our friends are coming for a visit.

cards.answerEn: for; fixed link in ir/venir de visita
cards.noteEn: In ir de visita or venir de visita, de connects the movement verb to visita. Natural English usually translates the whole expression as going or coming for a visit.

example.en: My aunt and uncle are coming for a visit.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, visita names an occasion when someone comes to see another person or place; it is not the verb form “visits.”
Tam is not a complete standard Spanish word. When the remaining letters are hidden or cut off, it can be the readable beginning of también.
Años is the plural of año. Keep the ñ: anos without it is a different word.

example.en: We lived there for two years.

cards.noteEn: Fwoosh is a comic sound effect for a fast rush through air or water.

example.es: El objeto cayó con un fwoosh.
example.en: The object fell with a fwoosh.

cards.answerEn: to me; marks the person who feels the pain
cards.noteEn: Doler is organized differently from English “hurt”: the painful thing controls the verb, while me, te, or le identifies who feels it.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish say who feels a pain?
cards.answerEn: Put me, te, le, nos, os, or les before a form of doler to identify the person who feels it.
cards.noteEn: The thing that hurts controls singular duele or plural duelen. In a completed construction, use ha or han followed by dolido; the short pronoun still names the person who feels the pain.

example.es: A Marta le duelen los pies.

cards.noteEn: Duele is used when one thing causes pain. The person feeling it is marked with me, te, le, nos, os, or les.
Dedo can mean either a finger or a toe. The surrounding context or the addition del pie makes the body part clear.

example.es: Me hice daño en un dedo del pie.
example.en: I hurt one of my toes.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “big toe”?
cards.answerEn: Use dedo gordo; add del pie when the context does not make the foot clear.
cards.noteEn: Dedo can mean either finger or toe. Gordo literally means fat or thick, but dedo gordo is the conventional name for the big toe. The adjective changes if the noun changes: dedos gordos for more than one.

example.es: Me lesioné el dedo gordo del pie.

cards.noteEn: Gordo normally means fat or thick. In the body-part name dedo gordo, it identifies the big toe.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Leído is the completed-action form of leer. It follows a form of haber in constructions such as he leído, “I have read.”

example.en: I have already read the message.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the masculine article inside el que (‘which’)
cards.noteEn: After a linking word such as en, el que can refer back to one masculine thing. El matches that earlier thing, while que introduces the added information.

example.es: Ese es el libro en el que aparece la foto.
example.en: That is the book in which the photo appears.

cards.noteEn: Era is a past form of ser used for a background state, description, or ongoing past situation. This form is called the imperfect.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.noteEn: Señal can name a posted sign, a transmitted signal, or evidence that points to a condition.

example.es: La fiebre puede ser una señal de infección.
example.en: A fever can be a sign of infection.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links señales to the evidence that follows
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses de before que after señal or señales when the following clause states what the sign indicates. English normally expresses the combination as ‘a sign that...’ without a separate word for de.

example.es: Es una señal de que funciona.
example.en: It is a sign that it works.

cards.noteEn: Metástasis is the medical term for disease spreading from its original site to another part of the body.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

cards.answerEn: yourself; marks the listener in darse un golpe
cards.noteEn: In te diste un golpe, te marks one familiar listener as the person who experienced the bump. Natural English often uses “yourself” or rearranges the body part.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone bumps or hurts themself?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of darse followed by un golpe.
cards.noteEn: Darse uses me, te, se, nos, os, or se to match the person who experiences the impact. Dar changes for the person and time; un golpe stays as the impact being experienced.

example.es: Luis se dio un golpe en el brazo.

cards.answerEn: you got; you gave yourself (in darse un golpe)
cards.noteEn: Diste is a completed-past form of dar for one familiar listener. With te and un golpe, it says that the listener bumped or hurt themself.

example.es: Te diste un golpe en la rodilla.

cards.noteEn: A golpe is a sudden impact. In darse un golpe, it commonly refers to bumping or hurting oneself.

example.es: Oí un golpe en la puerta.
example.en: I heard a knock at the door.

cards.noteEn: At the start of ¿y si...?, y helps introduce another possibility for someone to consider rather than simply joining two items with ‘and.’

cards.questionEn: How do you ask someone to consider “what if” a possibility happens?
cards.answerEn: Begin with ¿y si...? and state the possibility with an ordinary verb form.
cards.noteEn: The opening y does not merely mean ‘and’ here. Together with unaccented si, it presents a possible situation for consideration. It can introduce a suggestion or a worry.

example.en: What if we take the train?

cards.noteEn: Si has no accent when it introduces the possibility after y. Together, ¿y si...? asks someone to consider what might happen.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce a real or possible condition with “if”?
cards.answerEn: Use si without an accent, followed by an ordinary present-time verb form.
cards.noteEn: This pattern treats the condition as genuinely possible. Spanish normally does not put a future-tense verb directly after si in this kind of condition; the result can appear separately as a statement, prediction, or command.
Estimaron is the completed-past form of estimar for a plural subject.

cards.answerEn: of; links probabilidad to the possible action
cards.noteEn: After probabilidad, de can introduce an action in its unchanged dictionary form: la probabilidad de ganar.

example.es: La probabilidad de llegar a tiempo es baja.
example.en: The chance of arriving on time is low.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.noteEn: Hicieron is the irregular completed-past form of hacer for a plural subject.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Optimista has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns; optimistas is plural.
Seguramente often presents something as highly likely without making it completely certain.

example.en: She will probably arrive this afternoon.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.answerEn: is; may be (a possibility form of ser)
cards.noteEn: Sea is a form of ser used when something is presented as uncertain, possible, desired, or otherwise not stated as a plain fact. For a straightforward statement, the corresponding form is es.
After a negative verb, nada is commonly translated as “anything,” even though its basic meaning is “nothing.” Spanish keeps both negative words.
Dados is the masculine plural form of dado when it introduces several facts or circumstances to be considered.

example.en: Given the prices, we will buy less.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce facts or circumstances as things to consider?
cards.answerEn: Put dado, dada, dados, or dadas before the noun and make it match that noun.
cards.noteEn: In this pattern, dado means “given” or “considering,” not “die” or “dice.” It behaves like a describing word: dado el tiempo, dada la situación, dados los precios, dadas las circunstancias.

example.en: Given the circumstances, we will wait.

cards.noteEn: In health care, antecedentes are earlier conditions, diagnoses, or events that help a clinician assess the present situation.

example.en: The doctor reviewed my medical history.

cards.answerEn: we are going; we are going to
cards.noteEn: Vamos is the present form of ir for “we.” Before a and an action verb, it can announce a plan or near-future action.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)

cards.noteEn: At a restaurant, pedir is the ordinary verb for ordering food or drink. The same verb can mean asking for or requesting something elsewhere.

example.en: I am going to order the soup.

cards.noteEn: Completo describes something that covers all the needed parts or the whole scope.

cards.answerEn: in due course; then (in ya veremos, “we'll see”)
cards.noteEn: Ya has several uses. In ya veremos, it suggests that time or events will reveal the answer later.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.
Llamaremos keeps the full verb llamar and adds the -emos future ending for nosotros.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.
Resultados are the outcomes or answers produced by a process, test, calculation, or search.
Intenta tells one person addressed informally to try something. The same written form can mean “he, she, or formal you tries” in a statement; context marks it as a command here.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: No linking preposition is needed between the two verbs. Intento abrir means “I try to open,” and intentamos salir means “we try to leave.” The attempted action stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: We try to open the window.

cards.noteEn: Preocuparte combines preocupar with te, the matching marker for one familiar listener. The marker attaches to the end of the verb's dictionary form.

example.en: You do not have to worry.

cards.noteEn: Costar can describe difficulty rather than price. In cuesta followed by an action verb, the action is hard to do.

example.en: It is hard to admit a mistake.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that doing an action is difficult or takes effort?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of costar followed by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: When an action is the difficult thing, costar is normally singular: cuesta for the present, costó for a completed past event, or costará for the future. The following action stays in its basic form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir.

example.en: It is hard to stay calm.

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.
Estaba is a background-past form of estar. The subject can be I, he, she, or one formal you; here the unstated subject is the speaker.

example.en: I was tired after the trip.

cards.promptEs: estar + palabra que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe how someone or something is feeling or doing at a particular time?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by a describing word for the state.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to match who or what has the state: estoy means “I am,” está means “he, she, or it is,” and están means “they are.” The describing word matches the person or thing in gender and number: enfadado, enfadada, enfadados, or enfadadas. This pattern presents the quality as a condition or state; ser is normally used for identity or a defining description.
Calva describes a woman or feminine noun with no hair. The masculine form is calvo.

example.es: La actriz aparece calva en la escena.
example.en: The actress appears bald in the scene.

cards.questionEn: Where do common judgment words such as bueno or malo often go?
cards.answerEn: Put them before the noun when they give an overall evaluation: buena idea, mala noticia.
cards.noteEn: Spanish often puts a neutral descriptive word after its noun, but common evaluation words can come before it. The describing word still changes to match the noun: bueno becomes buena before a feminine singular noun.
Camino can be a physical path or, figuratively, a long process that leads to a result.

example.es: Fue un camino largo y difícil.
example.en: It was a long and difficult journey.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that one person or thing resembles another?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching small pronoun, a form of parecer, then a and the comparison target.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun changes with the person: me parezco, te pareces, se parece, nos parecemos. Parecer also changes for the person and time, while a always introduces who or what provides the comparison.

example.es: Esta casa se parece a la nuestra.

cards.noteEn: Parezco is the yo form of parecer. With me and a, parecerse a means to resemble someone or something.

cards.answerEn: like; required after parecerse before the comparison
cards.noteEn: Parecerse uses a before the person or thing that someone resembles.

example.es: El niño se parece a su abuelo.
example.en: The boy looks like his grandfather.

cards.noteEn: Hissssss imitates a sustained hiss. Repeated s letters make the sound last longer on the page.
Ya often means ‘already.’ In a question about an expected change, natural English commonly uses ‘yet’ or ‘by now.’

cards.answerEn: they are (in a state or condition)
cards.noteEn: Están is the present form of estar for a plural subject. Estar commonly describes a current condition.

cards.answerEn: how; marks the degree of a description in lo ... que

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something is sufficiently described in a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Put lo bastante before the describing word.
cards.noteEn: Lo bastante means “enough” or “sufficiently” before a description. Lo and bastante stay unchanged; the adjective still matches the person or thing described, as in lo bastante alta or lo bastante preparados.

example.es: Las cajas son lo bastante grandes.

cards.noteEn: After a verb or adjective, bastante can mean that the amount or degree is sufficient: no es bastante means “it is not enough.”

cards.answerEn: socialized; accustomed to social contact (masculine plural)
cards.noteEn: Socializados describes people or animals that have learned to interact comfortably with others.
Este can stand without a following noun when the nearby masculine person or thing is clear. Before a noun, the same form simply means ‘this,’ as in este libro.

cards.answerEn: may; might (as part of puede que)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something may or might be true or happen?
cards.answerEn: Use puede que, then put the following verb in a special possibility form.
cards.noteEn: The special form is called the subjunctive: it presents the following idea as possible rather than as a plain fact. Puede que stays fixed, while the next verb changes to match its own subject; for example, llega becomes llegue and es becomes sea.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes puede que (“may; might”)

cards.noteEn: Necesite is a present subjunctive form of necesitar. The subjunctive is a special verb form used after puede que when the need is only a possibility.
Visto is the irregular completed-action form of ver, ‘to see.’ After hemos, it helps form ‘we have seen.’
Ueeeeeee represents an excited cry during fast or playful movement. The repeated e letters stretch the sound.

example.en: She shouted “wheee!” on the way down.

cards.noteEn: Madrugar means getting up very early, usually because the day or an obligation starts early.

example.en: Tomorrow we have to get up early.

cards.noteEn: This drawn-out sound effect represents hesitation or reluctant agreement. Repeated letters stretch the groan.

example.en: She answered with a reluctant groan.

cards.noteEn: Buena has the feminine ending because it describes the feminine noun idea.
Idea ends in -a but is a feminine noun: una idea.
Ja represents a short burst of laughter in writing.

cards.answerEn: to them; marks the group that likes or dislikes something
cards.noteEn: With gustar, les identifies several people who experience the liking. It does not by itself mean “they.”

example.es: A mis amigos les gusta bailar.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone likes one thing or several things?
cards.answerEn: Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les for the person; then use gusta for one liked thing and gustan for more than one.
cards.noteEn: Spanish builds this as if the liked thing is pleasing to the person. The liked thing controls the verb: gusta este libro but gustan estos libros. You can clarify the person with a phrase beginning with a, such as a Marta or a quien.

example.es: A Marta le gustan los gatos.

cards.answerEn: are liked; appeal (used with plural liked things)
cards.noteEn: Gustan is plural because the things liked are plural. The person who likes them is identified separately by me, te, le, nos, os, or les.
Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cards.noteEn: Here le points back to a thing and functions as an indirect-object pronoun with prestar atención. A fuller a + noun phrase can state what le refers to.

example.es: A esta cuestión le presto mucha atención.
example.en: I pay close attention to this issue.

cards.promptEs: hacer una foto · hacerle una foto a alguien/algo
cards.answerEn: Use hacer una foto; to name what is photographed, use hacerle una foto a alguien or algo.
cards.noteEn: Hacer normally means “to make” or “to do,” but in this expression it corresponds to English “take.” Le and the words after a point to the person or thing in the photo. Tomar una foto is common in many other regions.
cards.questionEn: In Spain, how do you say “to take a photo” or “to take a photo of someone”?

example.es: Vamos a hacerle una foto al perro.
example.en: We are going to take a photo of the dog.

cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses hacer una foto where English uses “take a photo.” Hago is the yo form of hacer.

example.es: Le hago una foto al edificio.
example.en: I take a photo of the building.

cards.answerEn: of (marks what the photo is of)

cards.noteEn: Te can mean “to you” when you are the recipient or the person affected by an action. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.
Traigo is the present form of traer used when the speaker says yo. The middle of the verb changes: traer becomes traigo.

example.en: I am bringing bread for dinner.

cards.noteEn: The written accent distinguishes té, the drink, from te, a short pronoun meaning you or to you.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
In Spain, a napolitana is a flaky rectangular pastry commonly filled with chocolate or cream.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en serio (“seriously”)

cards.questionEn: How do you ask whether someone is really serious or whether something is actually true?
cards.answerEn: Use en serio to mean “seriously,” “really,” or “for real.”
cards.noteEn: En serio is a fixed expression. In a question, ¿En serio? often reacts with surprise or disbelief; in a statement, it can contrast sincerity with joking.

example.en: Are you really going to run tomorrow?

cards.answerEn: I am (in a state or condition)
to me; marks whose turn or responsibility it is
cards.noteEn: Before toca, me identifies the speaker as the person to whom the task falls.

example.en: It is my turn to pay.

cards.promptEs: tocarle a alguien + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action is someone's turn or responsibility?
cards.answerEn: Use a short recipient word such as me, te, le, nos, or les, then toca, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The short word identifies whose turn it is: me toca, te toca, le toca, nos toca, or les toca. The following action stays in its dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. A named person can be added with a, as in a Marta le toca.

example.en: It is our turn to clean the table.

cards.answerEn: is someone's turn; falls to someone to do
cards.noteEn: In tocarle a alguien hacer algo, toca does not mean physically touching. It says that an action is now that person's turn or responsibility.

example.en: Today it is my turn to cook.

cards.answerEn: to care for; to look after
cards.noteEn: Cuidar can be followed by de when it means taking responsibility for a person, animal, or thing.

example.es: Voy a cuidar de las plantas.
example.en: I am going to take care of the plants.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes care of a person, animal, or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of cuidar followed by de and the person or thing receiving care.
cards.noteEn: Cuidar changes for the person and time. De introduces what is being looked after: cuido de, cuidamos de, cuidará de.

example.en: Marta takes care of her grandfather.

cards.noteEn: When cuidar means looking after someone or something, de introduces the person or thing receiving care.

example.en: She takes care of her dog.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.answerEn: I am going to (before a + action)
cards.noteEn: Voy is the yo form of ir. Before a and an action verb, voy a announces a plan or near-future action.

cards.questionEn: What common exclamation can express surprise, shock, or amazement?
cards.noteEn: The words literally mean “my mother,” but speakers often use the complete expression as a reaction without referring to their mother. Tone and context determine whether it sounds alarmed, impressed, or overwhelmed.

cards.answerEn: my; part of the exclamation madre mía
cards.noteEn: Mía is the feminine singular possessive form matching madre. In ¡Madre mía!, the whole expression is a reaction rather than a literal statement about one's mother.

example.en: Goodness, what a lot of noise!

cards.questionEn: How do you say that no trace or sign of something can be found?
cards.answerEn: Use sin rastro de followed by the thing that cannot be found.
cards.noteEn: Rastro can literally mean a trail or trace. In this expression, sin rastro de says that no evidence remains. Before el, de contracts to del: sin rastro del problema.

example.es: La playa quedó sin rastro de basura.
example.en: The beach was left with no trace of litter.

cards.noteEn: Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.answerEn: really does; indeed, as part of sí que
cards.noteEn: The accent distinguishes affirmative sí from conditional si, “if.” Before que and a changed verb, sí adds strong confirmation rather than answering a yes-or-no question by itself.

example.en: Ana really does work a lot.

cards.questionEn: How do you strongly confirm that something really is true?
cards.answerEn: Put sí que before the changed verb to mean “really does,” “certainly is,” or “indeed.”
cards.noteEn: The accent on sí matters: sí confirms, while si without an accent means “if.” Que is part of this emphatic pattern and does not need a separate “that” in English. The following verb still changes normally for the person and time.

example.en: Marta really does know how to cook.

cards.answerEn: part of sí que, which strongly confirms what follows
cards.noteEn: In this pattern, que works with sí to add emphasis; it does not introduce an English “that” clause.
Síntoma is grammatically masculine despite ending in -a: el síntoma, los síntomas.
An articulación is the place where bones meet and movement can occur.

example.es: El frío le molesta en las articulaciones.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Perdiendo is the ongoing-action form of perder. After a form of estar, it presents the loss as in progress.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone loses their sight?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of perder followed by la vista.
cards.noteEn: Spanish normally uses the definite article la in this expression even when English uses “one's” or a possessive. Perder changes for the person and time; la vista stays fixed as the ability to see.

example.es: La enfermedad puede hacerle perder la vista.
example.en: The illness can cause him to lose his sight.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins de cerca, “up close”
cards.noteEn: De is fixed before cerca when describing a close viewing distance.

example.en: I want to see it up close.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is seen or examined up close?
cards.answerEn: Use the fixed expression de cerca.
cards.noteEn: De cerca describes a close viewing or observing distance. Keep both words together; cerca de has the different meaning “near” and normally introduces a following place, person, or thing.

example.es: Quiero mirar el mapa de cerca.
example.en: I want to look at the map up close.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “we” verb that is used with nos
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Nos marks the form for a group that includes the speaker. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

cards.questionEn: How can you say that a person or thing becomes or gradually grows a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of hacerse followed by the word that describes the new state.
cards.noteEn: The short marker and hacer form change with the subject: me hago, te haces, se hace, nos hacemos, and so on. The describing word matches the person or thing in number and, when its form changes, gender.

example.es: Las tardes se hacen más cortas.

cards.answerEn: we become (as part of nos hacemos + description)
cards.noteEn: Nos hacemos uses a form of hacer with nos to describe a gradual or chosen change. The following word names the new state.

example.es: Con los años nos hacemos más pacientes.
example.en: Over the years we become more patient.

cards.answerEn: not; begins ni tan mal, “not so bad”
cards.noteEn: In the conversational expression ni tan mal, ni helps soften or reverse the negative evaluation rather than joining a list.

example.es: Llegamos tarde, pero ni tan mal.
example.en: We arrived late, but it was not too bad.

cards.questionEn: How do you say conversationally that something is actually not too bad?
cards.noteEn: This informal expression gives a restrained positive assessment: the result may not be perfect, but it is acceptable or better than expected. It often stands alone after a pause or contrast.

example.es: No ganamos, pero ni tan mal.
example.en: We did not win, but it was not too bad.

cards.answerEn: bad; badly (in ni tan mal, “not so bad”)
cards.noteEn: Mal supplies the negative evaluation in ni tan mal, a conversational way to say that something turned out reasonably well.

example.es: El resultado no fue perfecto, pero ni tan mal.
example.en: The result was not perfect, but not too bad.

cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘everything that’ or ‘all that’ before saying what someone does?
cards.answerEn: Use todo lo que, then the part that says who does what.
cards.noteEn: Todo gives the idea of the complete amount. Lo que works together as ‘what’ or ‘that which,’ and the following verb changes normally for the person and time. In the prompt, the plus sign means ‘followed by.’

example.es: Leo todo lo que recomienda Marta.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.
Quería is a past form of querer used for a desire that existed at that past time. It does not say by itself whether the desire was fulfilled.
